reference_text:
Welcome to the course. We will work through each concept carefully, connect the
ideas step by step, and use practical examples to make technical topics easier
to understand. When we introduce a new method, focus first on the problem it
solves and why it is useful. For example, in machine learning, features are the
information we give the model, while the target is what we want it to predict.
Now consider a simple question: what changes when the data contains missing
values? We will think through the reason and then look at the code. In Python,
we can inspect the data, run one small step at a time, and explain what the
result means. The goal is to understand the logic, not simply memorize syntax.

slides.title: Functions
slides.transcript:
Welcome to Module 3. Functions help us turn repeated steps into named, reusable pieces of logic.

Instead of copying the same calculation again and again, we can define it once, give it a clear name, and reuse it with different values.

[tts-break]

By the end of this module, you should be comfortable defining a function, passing values into it, returning values from it, and combining small functions into a simple workflow.

slides.title: How to use this page
slides.transcript:
Work through the examples by reading, running, comparing, and then modifying the code.

When a function is introduced, try to identify three things: the inputs, the work being done, and the output. That input-process-output mindset makes functions much easier to understand.

[tts-break]

Use the browser editor to test small changes. Change one argument, rename one variable, or adjust one return value and see what happens.

slides.title: Learning path for Module 3
slides.transcript:
We begin with the basic structure of a function: define it, then call it.

Next, parameters make the function flexible, return values let us reuse results elsewhere, docstrings help explain the purpose, and function composition lets small pieces work together.

[tts-break]

The goal is to think of a function as a named analytical step. Inputs go in, the function performs one clear job, and useful results come back out.

slides.title: Why functions matter in analytics
slides.transcript:
Functions reduce repetition and make analytical code easier to manage.

Without functions, the same formula may be copied into several places. If the rule changes later, every copy has to be updated. With a function, the logic has one clear home.

[tts-break]

A name such as get_profit also communicates intent. It tells the reader what the code is supposed to do before they even inspect the details.

Functions are also easier to test because each small unit can be checked independently.

slides.title: A function has a definition and a call
slides.transcript:
Every function has two important moments: definition and call.

The definition tells Python what instructions belong to the function. Def show_welcome with parentheses creates the function and the indented lines become its body.

Calling show_welcome with parentheses tells Python to actually run those stored instructions.

[tts-break]

The colon and indentation matter. They mark where the function body begins and which lines belong to it.

slides.title: Code: a function with no parameters
slides.transcript:
Let’s begin with the smallest useful function.

Show_welcome takes no inputs. Its only job is to print a message. When Python reads the definition, it stores the instructions. Nothing is printed until we call show_welcome at the bottom.

[tts-break]

Change the message inside the function and run the cell again. The structure stays the same even though the behavior changes.

This example is simple, but the define-then-call pattern stays the same for more complex functions.

slides.title: Code: put a calculation inside a function
slides.transcript:
Now we put a calculation inside the function.

Sales and costs are created inside calculate_profit, and the function prints the difference. With one thousand in sales and eight hundred in costs, the result is two hundred.

[tts-break]

The limitation is that the numbers are fixed. Every call produces the same result.

That leads naturally to the next idea: parameters. Parameters let us keep the calculation but change the inputs.

slides.title: Parameters receive values
slides.transcript:
A parameter is a placeholder name inside the function definition. An argument is the actual value supplied when the function is called.

In def greet name, name is the parameter. When we call greet with Avery, Avery is the argument.

[tts-break]

Think of the parameter as an empty labeled slot. The argument is the value we place into that slot for one particular function call.

slides.title: Code: pass one argument
slides.transcript:
Here greet receives one argument.

The string Avery is assigned temporarily to the parameter name while the function runs. The f-string then inserts that value into the message.

[tts-break]

Change Avery to another fictional name or label. The function body does not need to change because the parameter makes the function flexible.

That is one of the main reasons functions are reusable.

slides.title: Code: pass two analytical inputs
slides.transcript:
Now the function receives two values: sales and costs.

When we call profit_report with twelve hundred fifty and nine hundred, those numbers flow into the two parameters. The function subtracts costs from sales, giving a profit of three hundred fifty dollars, then formats the result as money.

[tts-break]

Try a second call with two thousand and sixteen hundred. The same function should produce four hundred dollars in profit.

This is a common analytics pattern: define the metric once, then reuse it with different records.

slides.title: Default parameters supply common values
slides.transcript:
A default parameter gives the function a value to use when the caller does not provide one.

Here the default tax rate is ten percent. Calling calculate_tax with only five hundred uses that rate and returns fifty.

If we supply zero point one five as a second argument, the default is overridden and the tax becomes seventy-five.

[tts-break]

Defaults are useful for common assumptions, but they should be chosen carefully and documented clearly so the caller knows what will happen.

slides.title: return is different from print
slides.transcript:
Print and return are not the same thing.

Print displays a value for a person to see. Return sends a value back to the rest of the program so it can be stored, formatted, or used in another calculation.

[tts-break]

A useful rule is: if the result will be reused later, return is usually the better choice.

This distinction becomes very important as programs grow.

slides.title: Code: return a value
slides.transcript:
Get_profit returns the difference between sales and costs.

When we call it with one thousand and eight hundred, the returned value is two hundred. That value is stored in the variable profit and then printed.

[tts-break]

Because the value was returned, we could just as easily use it in a tax calculation, a margin calculation, or another report.

That makes return much more flexible than printing inside every function.

slides.title: Code: return more than one value
slides.transcript:
A function can return more than one result.

Summarize receives a list of values, finds the minimum and maximum, and returns both. Python then unpacks those two results into low and high.

With the current values, low is nine and high is twenty-one.

[tts-break]

This pattern is useful when one analytical function naturally produces several related metrics.

slides.title: Variables inside functions are local
slides.transcript:
Variables created inside a function usually belong to that function’s local workspace.

That means outside code does not automatically see them. This is helpful because the internal details of one function do not have to interfere with the rest of the program.

[tts-break]

When a useful result needs to leave the function, return provides a clean and explicit path.

Think of the function as a small workspace: inputs enter, local work happens, and selected outputs are returned.

slides.title: Code: catch a conversion error
slides.transcript:
Real data is messy, so functions often need a safe way to handle predictable problems.

Safe_integer tries to convert text to an integer. The string “42” converts successfully and returns forty-two. The text “forty-two” raises a ValueError, so the except block catches it and returns None instead.

[tts-break]

Try values such as “007”, “3.5”, and an empty string. Notice that not every string that looks numeric in some way is a valid integer.

This is a simple example of defensive programming.

slides.title: Code: add a docstring
slides.transcript:
A docstring documents the purpose of a function.

The triple-quoted text says that average returns the arithmetic mean of two numbers. That description becomes part of the function’s built-in documentation and can be accessed through average dot underscore underscore doc underscore underscore.

[tts-break]

Good documentation is especially useful when code will be reused by other people—or by you several months later.

Try rewriting the docstring in your own words while keeping the meaning accurate.

slides.title: Code: compose small functions
slides.transcript:
Small functions become powerful when we combine them.

The first function calculates profit. With sales of fifteen hundred and costs of ten fifty, profit is four hundred fifty.

The second function receives that profit and divides it by sales to calculate margin. Four hundred fifty divided by fifteen hundred gives thirty percent.

[tts-break]

This is function composition: one small result becomes the input to another small function.

Keeping each function focused on one job makes testing and reuse easier.

slides.title: Practice ladder
slides.transcript:
Use this practice ladder to build skill gradually.

Start with a no-parameter function, then add one parameter, then return a value. After that, practice handling a predictable error and combine defaults, documentation, and return values.

[tts-break]

At every level, explain the function in terms of input, process, and output. That explanation is more important than memorizing syntax.

slides.title: Practice code: foundation and building
slides.transcript:
The first practice function simply prints Hello. It has no parameters, so every call does the same thing.

The second function adds a name parameter. Now the same function can greet different people or labels.

[tts-break]

Run both examples, then change the argument in the second function. Compare how much more flexible the parameterized version is.

slides.title: Practice code: return and error handling
slides.transcript:
The first function returns the sum of two inputs. Twelve plus eight gives twenty, and that returned value is stored in result.

The second function tries to convert age text to an integer. If the conversion fails, it returns the message “Invalid age.”

[tts-break]

These examples combine two important habits: returning reusable results and handling expected errors without crashing the entire workflow.

slides.title: Practice code: defaults and documentation
slides.transcript:
This function combines several ideas at once.

Amount is required, rate has a default of eight percent, the docstring explains the purpose, and return sends the calculated tax back to the caller.

With an amount of two hundred fifty and the default rate, the result is twenty dollars.

[tts-break]

Call the function again with a ten percent rate and compare the result. This pattern can be adapted to discounts, fees, commissions, and many other calculations.

slides.title: Applied example: classify a temperature
slides.transcript:
Here we wrap a simple classification rule inside a function.

Check_fever receives a temperature. If the value is above ninety-eight point six, the function returns “Fever”; otherwise it returns “Normal.”

The loop then reuses that same rule for several values.

[tts-break]

The important programming idea is reusability. One rule can be applied repeatedly across a dataset.

This is only a coding example, not medical guidance.

slides.title: Mini project: reusable calculator function
slides.transcript:
The mini calculator combines parameters, return values, conditions, and a safety check.

The operation argument determines which branch runs. Add, subtract, and multiply return direct calculations. Divide checks whether the second value is zero before dividing.

If the operation is unknown, the function returns a clear message instead of failing silently.

[tts-break]

Try divide twenty by four, divide by zero, and an operation name that does not exist. Then extend the function with exponent or modulo.

slides.title: Function design checklist
slides.transcript:
A good function should have a clear name, clear inputs, one focused job, and a useful output.

Also think about predictable problems. Should the function validate something? Should it handle a conversion error? Would a future reader understand its purpose from the name and documentation?

[tts-break]

Small, focused functions are easier to test, easier to reuse, and easier to combine into larger workflows.

slides.title: Summary
slides.transcript:
Let’s bring the main ideas together.

Def creates a function. Parentheses call it. Parameters make inputs flexible. Return sends reusable results back to the program. Docstrings explain purpose, and small functions can be combined into larger workflows.

[tts-break]

Next, we move into lists and tuples so functions can work with structured collections of values.

[tts-break]

In Module 4, we’ll give those functions more structured data to work with. You’ll learn how lists and tuples store collections of values, how to access and update those values, and how to process an entire collection rather than working with one value at a time.
